questions.question: The analysis of a repository was made to run inside a temporary clone that is always deleted afterwards, rather than keeping a persistent checkout. What constraint made that the better choice?
variants: Why was analysing a repository in a throwaway clone that is always removed chosen over keeping a long-lived checkout of it?
What constraint favoured a disposable clone, deleted after every run, over a persistent local copy of the repository for analysis?
questions.reference_answer: The same code must run on a laptop, in CI or on a small hosted instance with limited disk and memory, and it analyses arbitrary repositories. A temporary clone, size-limited and always deleted, leaves nothing behind, and credentials never reach the output.

questions.question: The worker's analysis uses only the standard library, with no web framework, so it works as a library function and a command. What constraint made that the better choice over building it as a framework-based service?
variants: Why was the analysis worker written as a plain library and command rather than around a web framework?
What requirement favoured a framework-free, stdlib-only worker over a framework-based service?
questions.reference_answer: The same code has to run unchanged on a laptop, in CI and as the hosted platform's worker. Avoiding a framework keeps it dependency-free and portable across those hosts.

questions.question: Why does the worker record representative files for directory-only units rather than letting the question writer browse them?
variants: What limitation of the hosted question writer made precomputed file picks for directory-only units necessary?

When a unit names only directories, the worker precomputes a short list of representative files per unit instead of having the web app's question writer read the directory itself. What constraint forced that choice?
questions.reference_answer: The hosted question writer has no read tools, so a unit naming only directories would be quizzed with no code. The worker therefore picks the files ahead of time.

questions.question: If the analysis ran directly in a long-lived, persistent checkout instead of a temporary clone that is deleted afterwards, what first other behaviour of the surrounding system would have to be added?
variants: If analysed repositories were kept on disk permanently rather than cloned fresh and thrown away, what other part of the system would first need new handling?
If the worker stopped using a throwaway clone and reused a persistent working copy, what would the rest of the system first have to take on?
questions.reference_answer: Something would have to manage the stored checkouts: cleaning them up, bounding disk use, and keeping them at the right commit. With a transient clone, the size limits and the guaranteed deletion do this, which a small hosted instance relies on.

questions.question: If the part that picks representative files for a directory-only unit were dropped from the analysis step, which downstream consumer would first be left without code to show?
variants: If the analysis stopped recording representative files for units that name only directories, what consumer would first lose material?
Without the recorded representative files for directory-only units, which part of the system would first have nothing to show for them?
questions.reference_answer: The hosted web app's question writer, which has no read tools, would quiz such units with no code, or would have to fall back to listing the directory from GitHub at the pinned commit.

questions.question: If the analysis output were no longer written as a set of files, but handed straight back to the caller in memory, which other component that currently consumes the output would first need to change?
variants: If the worker stopped producing output files for a run, what consumer of those files would first have to change?
If the worker's results were returned in memory instead of written out, which downstream loader would first need to be rewritten?
questions.reference_answer: The loader that turns the worker's output files into database load statements (and the sample loader) reads the manifest and specs files, so it would need to take in-memory data instead.

questions.question: Why does the hosted analysis service turn away a second analysis request while one is already running?
variants: What constraint explains the service answering 'busy' to a new analysis while another is in progress?
Why does the hosted service run only one analysis at a time?
questions.reference_answer: It runs on a small free instance with about 512 MB of memory, so only one clone-and-analyse job fits at once.

questions.question: The hosted analysis service uses plain standard-library HTTP and REST clients instead of web frameworks or vendor SDKs. What constraint made that the better choice?

What constraint favoured stdlib REST clients over SDKs for the Render analysis service?
questions.reference_answer: The service has only a few JSON routes and runs on a small free instance, and the package is meant to keep no runtime dependency. Standard-library code is enough and keeps it dependency-free.

questions.question: The worker runs its own loop of model calls with read-only file tools instead of relying on the model gateway to provide file tools. What constraint forced that?
variants: Why does the worker drive the tool loop itself rather than using tools provided by the model gateway?
What property of the gateway made the worker run the read-tool loop on its own side?
questions.reference_answer: The gateway is a plain Messages API proxy with no file tools of its own and one model call per request. So the worker must supply the read tools over the clone and loop itself.

questions.question: The service writes to the database with the signed-in person's own token rather than a privileged service-level key. What constraint made that the better choice?
variants: Why does the worker use the user's token for database writes instead of a service-role key?
What policy made per-user tokens preferable to an all-powerful key for the worker's database access?
questions.reference_answer: Apps are never given the service-role key. Using the person's token means row-level security applies, so rows the worker writes belong to that person.

questions.question: If the hosted service's hand-written web calls to Supabase were replaced by the official Supabase client library, what first project-level property would change?
variants: If the service used an official Supabase SDK instead of hand-written HTTP calls, what would change about the package's dependencies?
What packaging property would be lost if the Render service adopted the Supabase SDK rather than plain standard-library REST calls?
questions.reference_answer: The package would no longer be free of runtime dependencies, since it currently relies only on the standard library. The same would hold for a web framework or other SDKs.

questions.question: If the model calls were made through a provider SDK that ran its own file-reading agent, instead of the service's own loop, what part of the service would no longer be needed?
variants: If an SDK agent handled file reading for the model, which of the service's own parts would become redundant?
What would become unnecessary if the model's tool use were handled by a provider's built-in agent rather than the service's loop?
questions.reference_answer: The service's own tool loop and its read-only file tools over the clone, with their path checks and size caps, would be unneeded. They exist because the gateway proxies a single model call and offers no file tools.

questions.question: If the service were changed to act with a privileged database key instead of each person's own token, which database protection would the worker's writes first bypass?
variants: If the worker used a service-level key rather than the signed-in person's token, what protection would stop applying to its writes?
Switching the worker from the person's token to an admin key would first sidestep which safeguard?
questions.reference_answer: Row level security: with the person's token, rows the worker writes are that person's own. A privileged key would skip that ownership enforcement.

questions.question: Why must a received GitHub delivery be signature-verified before anything acts on its routing result?
variants: What would be at risk if a delivery were routed and acted on without first checking its signature?
Why does the receiver check the shared-secret signature on a delivery before queuing analyses or checks?
questions.reference_answer: Without verification anyone could forge a delivery and trigger analyses, checks or acknowledgements; the signature proves it came from GitHub with the shared secret.

questions.question: Webhook verification and routing were written as pure functions with no web framework or database, instead of inside a particular receiving service. What constraint made that the better choice?
variants: Why is webhook routing kept free of any framework or database rather than built into one receiver?
What requirement favoured pure, host-agnostic routing logic over logic embedded in a specific web service?
questions.reference_answer: Different hosts, such as a platform function or the worker, can receive the delivery. Pure functions can be shared by all of them and tested against recorded events.

questions.question: The pull-request check is advisory by default, with only an opt-in soft block that a lead can clear, rather than a hard block tied to quiz scores. What constraint motivated that?
variants: Why does the pull-request check pass by default instead of blocking changes outright?
Why was a lead-clearable soft block chosen over a hard gate based on the author's understanding?
questions.reference_answer: Nothing should wait on the author's quiz score, so a hard block is rejected. A lead's acknowledgement can clear the optional soft block, keeping a human in the loop.

questions.question: Who is a lead is left to the caller to say instead of being decided inside the routing logic. What constraint made that the better choice?
variants: Why does webhook routing not decide for itself who counts as a lead?
Why is the role lookup delegated to the host instead of built into the router?
questions.reference_answer: Roles live wherever the host keeps them, and the routing code has no database. Letting the caller supply the role keeps routing pure and portable.

questions.question: If webhook routing were folded into a web handler that also did the database and network work, what first property of the routing would be lost?
variants: If routing GitHub events were mixed with the code that performs the actions, what would be lost?
What property of the event routing would be lost if it were no longer separate from its side effects?
questions.reference_answer: It could no longer be tested on its own with recorded event fixtures, and no longer be reused by whatever receives the delivery (a platform function or the worker). The router currently only decides what to do and leaves doing it to the caller.

questions.question: If the pull-request check were made a hard block on the author's quiz score, what other part of the system would first have to supply new information?
variants: If the check blocked merges until the author passed a quiz, what component would first need to provide new data?
If the check became a hard gate on quiz results, what would the check need from the rest of the system?
questions.reference_answer: The quiz evidence (understanding record) would have to be available to the check as a pass/fail requirement. Currently the check is advisory or soft-blocked and only a lead's acknowledgement clears it.

questions.question: If who counts as a lead were decided inside the routing code instead of by the caller, what other part would have to change?
variants: If the router owned the notion of lead roles, what would have to move into it?
If role lookup were no longer supplied by the caller, what would the routing need that it does not have?
questions.reference_answer: Whatever stores the roles would have to be reachable by the router, tying the router to the host's role storage. At present roles live wherever the host keeps them, so the routing stays free of a database.

questions.question: The hosted app stores its data in Supabase Postgres rather than in its own API with its own database. What constraint made that the better choice?

What did Supabase supply that made a self-built backend unnecessary?
questions.reference_answer: Auth, row-level security and storage come with Supabase, so no separate backend had to be built. That fits an app that is mostly per-user rows.

questions.question: Alongside the hosted Postgres schema, a SQLite twin of the schema is kept. What constraint made that the better choice?
variants: Why keep a SQLite copy of the Postgres schema?
What need is served by a SQLite twin of the hosted database schema?

questions.question: Analyses are loaded through generated SQL that deletes the existing analysis for that repository, commit and owner and then reinserts it in one transaction, rather than inserting blindly. What constraint made that better?
variants: Why does the loader replace an existing analysis in a transaction instead of just inserting?
What requirement does the delete-and-reinsert loader satisfy?
questions.reference_answer: The load must be safely repeatable: running it again for the same repository, commit and owner should yield the same state, not duplicates. The transaction keeps the replacement atomic.

questions.question: If Supabase were replaced by the team's own API with its own database, what first built-in capability would the system have to build itself?
variants: If the app dropped Supabase for its own backend, what capability would have to be created first?
What did Supabase supply out of the box that a self-built API would have to replace?
questions.reference_answer: Sign-in and per-user access control, which Supabase supplies as auth and row level security (plus storage). A custom backend would have to implement them.

questions.question: If the SQLite twin of the schema were removed, which part of the development process would first lose its test target?

What would the schema tests lose if the lightweight second database copy were dropped?

questions.question: If the SQL loader were no longer idempotent, what first problem would appear when the same analysis is loaded twice?
variants: If loading an analysis twice were not safe, what would happen to the stored data?

questions.reference_answer: Duplicate analysis rows for the same repository and commit would accumulate, since the current loader deletes the matching analysis and reinserts it in one transaction.

What favoured starting from the HintWise template over a framework-based rewrite?

questions.question: The web app does model-backed work in serverless functions that check the caller's token, rather than calling the model directly from the browser. What constraint made that the better choice?

What requirement made server-side functions better than direct browser calls for model work?

questions.question: What gap does the GitHub directory fallback fill for directory-only units?
variants: For directory-only units, the web app falls back to listing the directory from GitHub at the pinned commit when no recorded file list exists. What constraint made that the better choice?
Why does the web app list a directory from GitHub when the specs lack a file list?

questions.question: If the web app were rebuilt with a framework such as React instead of plain TypeScript, what first part of the project's existing foundation would be given up?
variants: If a framework replaced the plain TypeScript front end, what would be given up first?
What reuse would be lost by switching the front end from the template's vanilla approach to React?
questions.reference_answer: The reuse of the existing HintWise app template, which the app was imported from, would be lost, along with its UI code built without a framework.

questions.question: If the serverless functions were replaced by server rendering, which party would first need to hold the secrets the browser lacks today?
variants: If pages were rendered on a server instead of through serverless functions, what would first need handling of secrets?
If server rendering replaced the function endpoints, what would have to take over the work the functions do?
questions.reference_answer: The server itself would have to do what the functions do now: check the person's token against the database, and call the model and GitHub for questions, grading, excerpts and trees.

questions.question: If users' model keys were held by the server instead of being supplied by each user, what first other part of the system would have to change?

If model access were paid for centrally rather than by each user's key, what new capability would be needed?
questions.reference_answer: The system would need server-side key storage and cost controls, such as usage caps, because each user no longer carries their own cost and key.

questions.question: Why must the browser get code excerpts through the site's own server API instead of fetching them from GitHub directly?

Why does the hosted app proxy file contents through its server API rather than letting the page call GitHub?

questions.question: The server API logic was written as plain request-to-response code that both the hosting platform's function runtime and the local development server call, rather than being written separately for each. What constraint made sharing one implementation the better choice?
variants: Why was the server API written as web-standard request/response code shared by the hosted functions and the local dev server instead of separate implementations?
What constraint favored one shared implementation of the API over separate hosted and local versions?
questions.reference_answer: The local dev server, the preview and the end-to-end tests needed to exercise exactly the code the live site runs, so one implementation avoids drift between a hosted copy and a dev copy.

questions.question: The server functions can read repository files either from GitHub or from a local clone when fakes are on. What constraint made this switchable choice better than always calling GitHub?
variants: Why can the file-fetching part read from a local clone instead of only GitHub?
What constraint motivated giving the GitHub-reading code a local-clone mode?
questions.reference_answer: Dev, preview and end-to-end runs must work offline and deterministically without hitting GitHub (and its rate limit) or needing real credentials, so a local clone stands in for GitHub.

questions.question: The GitHub tree listing is kept in memory per repository and commit rather than refetched on each request or stored in a database. What constraint made that the better choice?
variants: Why is the tree listing cached in memory keyed by repository and commit, not stored persistently?
What property of a tree at a given commit makes a short in-memory cache sufficient?
questions.reference_answer: A tree at a given commit never changes, so caching per commit is always valid and saves calls against GitHub's unauthenticated rate limit, with no need for persistent storage.

questions.question: If the server API handlers were no longer written as plain request-to-response code shared with the local dev server, but tied to Netlify's own runtime, what first other part of the system would have to change?
variants: If the API handlers depended on Netlify's runtime instead of standard request and response objects, which other component would break first?
What would the local development and preview server have to do differently if the API handlers became Netlify-runtime-specific?
questions.reference_answer: The local dev/preview server plugin that mounts the same handlers at the API path would have to change, since it could no longer call them directly. The same-code-in-dev guarantee, which the browser end-to-end walkthrough relies on, would be lost.

questions.question: If the code excerpts were fetched by the browser straight from the code host instead of through a server function, what first other part of the system would have to change?

What safeguard would have to move if the excerpt proxy were removed?
questions.reference_answer: The page's security policy for allowed connections would need to permit the code host, and the safeguards on path, commit and size now enforced server-side would have to move into the browser. The fake-clone reading used in tests would also be bypassed.
